issues.issue: The recital closes with a stray quotation mark and the phrase "(“Agreement”) as further defined below," although no further definition of "Agreement" appears anywhere in the instrument. The defect is cosmetic and does not change who the parties are or what is promised.

The clause states that "neither party shall in any event be held liable or accountable for any obligations incurred by either party other than as specified herein," which read literally would excuse each party from obligations it actually incurred. The independent-contractor substance is otherwise standard.

"PRODUCTS" is defined circularly as only those products COMPANY authorizes, with no list or exhibit fixing them, so the subject matter of the sale is defined by one party's unilateral say-so. That leaves the scope of the distributorship indeterminate at any given moment.

TERRITORY is defined by reference to Exhibit "A", whose handwritten territory entry is not legible in the instrument, and the same sentence restricts sales to "retail grocery store outlet customers only". The definition therefore cannot be applied without extrinsic evidence.

The "grocery store retail outlets only" limit sits against 3(ii)(a)(i)(B)-(C) (Kmart and COMPANY-approved customers) and the final paragraph of Exhibit "B" grandfathering existing customers in excluded channels. The AUTHORIZED CHANNEL OF TRADE is thus wider in those provisions than in this definition.

"Good Industry Practice" is defined as standards "universally accepted and followed in the baking industry" followed by a non-exhaustive list, so the reach of the general standard beyond the four listed items is open. Because 12(iii)(b) makes breach of Good Industry Practice a termination ground, the boundary matters.

"shall continue for until December 31, 2008" is ungrammatical, and the last sentence ("or until terminates in accordance with paragraph 12") is missing its subject; the successor-agreement right is also expressed without any limit on how many successors or on COMPANY's obligation to offer one. Whether DISTRIBUTOR held an enforceable perpetual renewal right or merely a right to sign whatever form COMPANY then offered turns on these words.

The sentence permitting either party to terminate after December 31, 2008 on ninety days' notice cannot be squared with Paragraph 12(i), which permits ninety-day termination only "for good cause" or on a change in COMPANY's DSDD business. One reads as termination at will, the other as termination only for cause.

COMPANY's unilateral power to "determine the TERRITORY and AUTHORIZED CHANNEL OF TRADE" is hard to reconcile with Paragraph 15(iii) (Modification), which permits amendment only by a written instrument executed by both parties, since TERRITORY is fixed by Exhibit "A" incorporated into the Agreement. It also overlaps the Exhibit "B" revision mechanism in 3(ii)(d).

"grocery store retail outlets only" is followed by the open-ended category "specific customers as approved by COMPANY", so the closed word "only" and the expandable third item pull against each other. Whether a given account (e.g. a supermarket inside another format) is a "grocery store retail outlet" is left undefined.

The permitted-customer list conflicts with the closing paragraph of Exhibit "B", which allows DISTRIBUTOR to continue serving its existing customers in expressly excluded channels until further notice. Read together it is unclear whether grandfathered accounts are authorized sales or breaches under 3(ii)(d).

The in-store service duties "will consist of, but are not limited to" four enumerated activities, leaving the reach of the unstated remainder to be filled by ejusdem generis. "Guaranteed sales" is then given its own bespoke definition that may not match trade usage.

The final sentence — "DISTRIBUTOR must meet certain other guidelines that the COMPANY may determine in its discretion from time to time" — is an unbounded catch-all appended to two specific prohibitions, with no content and no notice requirement. Its reach beyond wholesaling and bid processes cannot be measured.

A duty to adhere to standards "promulgated, altered, amended or modified by COMPANY" unilaterally sits awkwardly with Paragraph 15(iii) (Modification), which allows amendment only by a writing executed by both parties. Whether COMPANY-issued policies become contract terms is left open.

The prohibition on selling to "retail stores serviced by the Kellogg's Snacks DSD division" is a floating, COMPANY-controlled carve-out that is not reflected in the TERRITORY definition (I(iii)) or in Exhibit "B"'s list of excluded channels. Which stores fall inside it can change without any contractual mechanism.

As written the sentence forbids sales "to any CUSTOMERS or in any AUTHORIZED CHANNEL OF TRADE other than as stated herein" — using the defined terms for the permitted customers and channel, so the prohibition reads back on the very sales the Agreement authorises. "[A]ny such changes are effective thirty days of receipt" is also missing a preposition.

Allowing COMPANY to revise Exhibit "B" "without notice in the sole discretion of COMPANY" while the exhibit is "incorporated herein" cannot easily be squared with Paragraph 15(iii) (Modification), which requires a writing executed by both parties. The clause also says changes take effect on receipt though revision is "without notice".

The clause promises "commercially reasonable efforts to resolve any conflicts" in sales conflicting with "Paragraph 3(a)(i) above", but there is no Paragraph 3(a)(i); the intended reference is 3(ii)(a)(i). The cross-reference error leaves the triggering event uncertain.

Making COMPANY's decision on customer and channel status "final and binding" sits against 3(ii)(d)'s promise of commercially reasonable efforts to resolve conflicts and against the grandfather sentence of Exhibit "B", which appears to give DISTRIBUTOR a vested entitlement to existing accounts. Whether COMPANY can extinguish that entitlement by fiat is the open question.

The unqualified undertaking that COMPANY "shall deliver the PRODUCTS" cannot be squared with 3(ii)(g), which lets COMPANY cancel any delivery in whole or in part in its sole discretion, cut quantities and discontinue items without liability. Read together the delivery obligation may be illusory.

"[A]ny cause beyond its control" is given no enumeration and is qualified by "cannot be overcome by reasonable diligence", so the events covered are defined only by an abstract standard. Force majeure boundaries are a common site of construction.

An unfettered right to cancel any delivery and to "cut" volumes without liability is difficult to reconcile with 3(ii)(e) ("COMPANY shall deliver the PRODUCTS") and with Paragraph 6, which requires COMPANY to ship so products are available on the scheduled date. Together they leave no ascertainable supply obligation.

The reserved right to sell within the TERRITORY "to customers other than the CUSTOMERS" and to deliver to a CUSTOMER's central warehouse overlaps the exclusivity disclaimers in 3(i) and 3(ii)(d); whether central-warehouse deliveries to a CUSTOMER strip DISTRIBUTOR of its service role is unaddressed. It also touches the grandfather sentence of Exhibit "B".

The general ban on products "which may reasonably be deemed as injurious to the sales potential of PRODUCTS" including "competitive cookie, cracker, and wholesome snack products" is then contradicted by a specific authorisation of TastyKake and Stella D'oro "cake, cookie, cracker and snack products", so the general prohibition and the enumerated exception overlap. "[W]holesome snack" and the garbled "shall promptly reply and not unreasonably withheld its consent" compound the uncertainty.

The parties "agree to share in the cost" of electronic data processing equipment without stating any allocation, and reimbursement is to be "on such terms and in such amounts as COMPANY reimburses its other DSDD distributors", a benchmark internal to COMPANY. Both undertakings lack an ascertainable measure.

"[S]hort dated" is defined as products "whose expiration dates are approaching in the near future", a definition that supplies no boundary, and the 45-day proviso then does different work depending on where that boundary sits. The vagueness is on the face of the definition.

The standard is "such standards ... as are conducive to maintenance and furtherance of the reputation and sale of the PRODUCTS", which states an aspiration rather than a measurable duty. It is nevertheless enforceable through the 12(iii)(b) termination route.

"[A]ssist COMPANY in providing or obtaining information as to the credit standing of itself" leaves "itself" grammatically pointing at COMPANY rather than DISTRIBUTOR. The mistake is obvious enough that context probably cures it.

DISTRIBUTOR bears all receivable collection risk "with exception for accounts where COMPANY is responsible for accounts receivable (e.g. Kmart)", an exception identified only by a single illustrative example with no list. Which other accounts fall inside it cannot be determined from the text.

The one-way indemnity here runs only from DISTRIBUTOR, whereas Paragraph 13(i) makes indemnification mutual for breach and for acts of either party's agents; the two indemnities overlap without a priority rule. Paragraph 12(v)'s damages cap also does not say whether it limits indemnity claims.

The arithmetic depends on "the approximate $30,000.00 which COMPANY owes DISTRIBUTOR", yet the stated net of $5,250.71 requires exactly $30,000; the date of the underlying writing is also garbled ("November [4 2006)"). Whether the credits were settled at exactly $30,000 or remain open is left unresolved.

Price and payment are left "at such terms as established by COMPANY from time to time", so the central commercial term is set unilaterally with no formula or benchmark. The provision is essentially an agreement to accept whatever COMPANY sets.

The thirty-day notice requirement for changing terms sits against 4(v) Payment Terms, which fixes net thirty/one percent fifteen days, and against 4(ii), which lets COMPANY change prices "at any time". Which controls a mid-term change is not stated.

The clause both requires revision of prices "upon thirty (30) days written notice" and reserves "the right at any time to issue new price lists and to change the prices" in the same sentence. The two limbs cannot both be given full effect.

Title passing "absolutely" on delivery is in tension with Paragraph 12(iv)'s repurchase option and 12(vi)'s security interest and self-help repossession right over PRODUCTS in DISTRIBUTOR's possession. Whether COMPANY retains any proprietary claim to delivered goods is not squarely resolved.

DISTRIBUTOR must pass through 100% of the promotional allowance while bearing 25% of it, so the clause both grants and takes back part of a discount; whether the 25% is a cost or merely an accounting entry is unexplained. The worked example illustrates the arithmetic but not the legal effect.

The cash discount is payable "if a payment is made within designated number of days the COMPANY has allowed in its current credit terms" — a missing article and an undefined external reference, with no percentage stated. The entitlement therefore has no fixed content.

The undefined cash discount here overlaps 4(v) Payment Terms, which fixes a one percent discount for payment within fifteen days (twenty by EFT). Whether the two are the same discount or cumulative is unstated.

The fixed net-thirty and one-percent-fifteen-day terms sit against Paragraph 4's opening sentence allowing COMPANY to establish and change terms unilaterally on thirty days' notice, and against the separately defined Cash Discount in 4(iv). No priority is stated.

The obligation to make products available on the scheduled delivery date (plus or minus five days) is contradicted by 3(ii)(g), which disclaims all liability for delays, cuts and cancellations in COMPANY's sole discretion. The only remedy given here for an out-of-stock item is reordering.

Making replacement or credit the "sole remedy" for breach of the Paragraph 8 guarantee cuts across Paragraph 13(i), which requires each party to indemnify the other for losses caused by breach of the Agreement. The two remedies provisions are not subordinated to one another.
